newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein's Adams calls for end to hijackings.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein's Adams calls for end to hijackings.

text.p: Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing, called on Roman Catholic youths on Monday to stop car hijackings and burnings and found himself personally involved when a truck was seized in West Belfast.
Adams said he was on his way to a meeting when he came across a builder's truck that had been hijacked in the city's Catholic Andersonstown heartland.
"We just discovered that some young people had hijacked this lorry and we are trying to return it to its owner," he told Reuters.

Hundreds of cars, trucks and buses have been hijacked and burned in Catholic nationalist violence that swept Northern Ireland after members of the Protestant Orange Order were allowed to march through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Adams and his chief negotiator, Martin McGuinness, made their appeals after one of the worst nights of violence in Northern Ireland for years.
"There's a lot of anger in this community, justifiable righteous anger. We have to channel that anger into actions which do not deflect attention from the British government's action," Adams said.
As he spoke, crowds gathered at the side of the Andersonstown Road and cars picked their way along the pavement past the stranded truck.
Adams called upon nationalists "to be calm, to be disciplined, to refuse to accept the burden of second class citizenship".
The Sinn Fein leader, a distinctively tall and beared figure, was driven away as a police and British amry patrol in armoured Land Rovers made its way towards him.
Despite his appeals, locals were still burning vehicles only a short distance from where he was speaking.
Clouds of oily smoke drifted into the sky as two Belfast city buses were set ablaze in a staunchly Roman Catholic area.
Earlier, Adams told a Belfast news conference: "We want to call for an end to the hijackings and burnings."
His and McGuinness's appeals were the first public attempt by Sinn Fein for calm since the province began counting down to the climax of the Protestant marching season next Sunday.
Across the province Catholic youths used the well-worn tactic of hijacking cars, setting them alight and then stoning or throwing petrol bombs at emergency services and police.
In the border town of Newry alone 221 vehicles were hijacked in 36 hours, police figures showed.
Adams, whose party shares the Irish Republican Army's goal of ending British rule of Northern Ireland, called for "calm and dignified protest."
He made no mention of IRA sniper attacks on British security forces which took place during the night in one of the biggest displays of IRA firepower for years.
The IRA and a breakaway group, the Irish National Liberation Army, fired dozens of shots at security forces overnight. A policewoman was injured in the face, but not seriously.

McGuinness, who issued an appeal to Irish nationalists on Sunday to "take to the streets" in protest, said in a statement that the "anger and frustration of nationalists in Northern Ireland is understandable."
But he added: "The riots and damage to property is counter-productive."
